Act 24

How Hawaiʻi’s 2026 income tax law changes state revenue, and who pays more or less, compared with the Act 46 schedule it replaced.

Hawaiʻi Appleseed · Model run September 24, 2026 · Tax years 2027 to 2031

$876 million
More revenue over five years, tax years 2027 to 2031, than Act 46 would have raised.
$127 million
In tax year 2027, the first year the new brackets apply.
$78

$43,714
Average increase for households with income above $1 million in 2027.

What Act 24 Changed

ACT 24 REWROTE THE INCOME TAX BRACKETS that Act 46 of 2024 had scheduled for the rest of the decade.12 It cut two rates that most working households pay and raised the rates on income above $350,000 for joint filers ($262,500 for heads of household, $175,000 for single filers), adding a 13 percent bracket above $1 million ($750,000 and $500,000).

Table 1 shows the changes for joint filers. The lower-bracket cuts are the same in every year. The increases at the top grow in 2029, when Act 46 would have lowered those rates again and Act 24 holds them where they are.

Act 24 also capped, ended or repealed several tax credits. These estimates score the three largest changes. It caps the renewable energy technologies income tax credit at $40 million a year, limits it to filers with income under $175,000 (single) or $350,000 (joint), and ends new credits after tax year 2029.3 It ends the capital goods excise tax credit after tax year 2027 and speeds up the phase-out of the research activities credit.

What It Raises

COMPARED WITH ACT 46, Act 24 raises an estimated $127 million in tax year 2027, rising to $214 million by 2031, for $876 million over five years.4

Two pieces add up to that total, shown in Figure 1. The bracket changes raise $420 million over the five years after accounting for high-income filers reporting less income when rates rise. The credit changes save the state $456 million, most of it from the renewable energy credit ($358 million). Credit savings jump in 2030, the first year no new renewable energy credits are allowed.

How sure are these numbers? The low and high scenarios vary how strongly top earners respond to higher rates, how fast top incomes grow, and how much demand there is for the renewable energy credit. Over five years they range from $788 million to $1,066 million. One channel is not yet in these figures: some business owners may pay tax through their business instead of on their own returns to avoid the new top rate, which would lower the bracket gain.

Who Pays More and Who Pays Less

MOST HOUSEHOLDS PAY A LITTLE LESS. The lower rates on income between about $29,000 and $48,000 of taxable income for joint filers reach most working households. In tax year 2027, the middle 20 percent of households save an average of $78 and the next 20 percent $92. Households with income under $350,000 save $32 million in all.

The increase falls on the top. Households with income above $1 million pay an average of $43,714 more, and the top 20 percent as a group pay $108 million more. Figure 2 shows the average change for each fifth of households, and Table 3 by income.

The credit changes are not in these figures. They fall on the relatively few filers who claim the renewable energy, capital goods and research credits, not evenly across income groups, and the model estimates them in total rather than household by household.

Act 24 Against the Law Before Act 46

ACT 24 IS SMALL NEXT TO THE TAX CUT IT AMENDED. Act 46 of 2024 raised the standard deduction and widened the brackets in steps through 2031. Measured against the law before Act 46, it will cost the state about $1,178 million a year by 2031 on this model’s static estimate. Act 24 recovers $170 million of that, about 14 percent.5

This model’s estimate of Act 46’s cost runs 14 to 21 percent below the Department of Taxation’s own figure, $1.45 billion by fiscal year 2032, largely because survey data miss nonresident filers and some business income.6 That gap largely cancels when comparing Act 24 with Act 46, since both are scored on the same population, which is why the estimates above use that comparison.7

How These Estimates Are Made

THE MODEL BUILDS a synthetic population of about 39,990 Hawaiʻi tax units from the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey microdata (HI 5yr 2020-24), calibrated to Department of Taxation statistics, and computes each unit’s tax under both laws for every year. Filers with income above $1 million, whom survey data miss, are added from IRS and state tax statistics.

High earners are assumed to report less taxable income when their rates rise, and a few to move away; those responses are in the bracket figures. The credit changes are scored against projected claims under the old rules. The middle scenario is the recommended one. The full method, every parameter and each revision are documented with the code.7

Download the data

  • fiscal_by_scenario.csv: revenue by tax year and scenario, with every component
  • distribution_quintile.csv: change by fifth of households, 2027 to 2031
  • distribution_income_class.csv: change by income class, 2027 to 2031
  • vs_pre_act46.csv: Act 46 and Act 24 compared with pre-Act 46 law
  • manifest.json: run parameters, input vintages and code version
